sources.citation: van der Hulst, Harry & Rob Goedemans. 2010. Word accent systems in the languages of Asia. In van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds.), A Survey of Word Accentual Patterns in the Languages of the World, ch. 10, pp. 509-599. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sources.citation: Kumar, Anjali V. 2024. A descriptive study of the Koraga language of Kasaragod. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Central University of Kerala (guide S. Thennarasu). xxii+261 pp. Shodhganga hdl 10603/650398.
sources.note: Nothing. Chapter 3 Phonology (pp. 91-130, text) is segmental only: 27 consonants, 7 vowels + length, diphthongs, syllable template (C)(C)V(C)(C), phonotactics, clusters. 'Suprasegmental' appears only generically in the chapter's opening paragraph; no stress statement. Ch. 1 literature review (read) names no work treating Koraga prosody.

sources.note: Nothing found. Chapter II gives vowel/consonant/diphthong lists with examples (place and manner of articulation tables), then a phrasebook and vocabulary; Malayalam keyword search (uunnal, balaaghaatam, svanima etc.) and a skim of ch. II found no stress/accent statement.

sources.citation: Shetty, Ramakrishna T. 1978. Koraga Grammar (A descriptive study of a Dravidian dialect). PhD thesis, Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute / University of Poona (guide H. S. Biligiri). vi+375 pp. Shodhganga hdl 10603/145443. [Describes the Ande dialect, Mangalore; published 2008 as Koraga Grammar, Kuppam: Dravidian University]
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Chapter 1 Phonology (38 pp., scanned and read: inventory, contrasts, allophony, distribution, clusters) has no stress/accent section or statement; only 'The voiceless stops are tense and slightly aspirated in the initial position' and (vowels, 1.3.2.2) 'The short vowels are half-long finally'. Introduction p. 2 states explicitly: 'The description of intonation and juncture, however, is not attempted in this grammar.'

sources.citation: Bhat, D. N. Shankara. 1971. The Koraga Language. (Deccan College Linguistic Survey of India Series 7.) Poona: Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute. 136 pp. [archive.org id unset0000unse_k9c8, Servants of Knowledge collection]
sources.note: Nothing. The phonology sections for Onti (pp. 4-5), Tappu (pp. 21-22) and Mudu (pp. 33-34) give phonemic inventory, allophony notes and contrast pairs only; the comparative chapter (pp. 41ff) treats segmental correspondences. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere (full-text search plus reading of all three phonology sections).
